strengths: Introduces a simple, interpretable, and architecture-robust two-sample classifier metric m(pX) for quantifying distributional symmetry breaking, with clean theoretical interpretation (optimal Bayes accuracy under finite-orbit models) and extensive ablations showing robustness to model size/dataset size.

Provides a genuinely novel theoretical analysis of invariant ridge regression under non-invariant data distributions, extending Elesedy & Zaidi (2021) to both under- and over-parameterized regimes, showing (counter to common intuition) that data augmentation/symmetrization can hurt even for truly invariant ground-truth functions; theory is carefully derived with deterministic equivalents from random matrix theory and validated in simulation (Figure 3).

Very broad and thorough empirical study across many real-world domains (QM9, QM7b, rMD17, OC20, ModelNet40, MNIST, an LLM materials dataset), consistently revealing surprisingly high distributional symmetry breaking, which is a valuable empirical finding for the community.

Introduces a complementary task-dependent metric t(pX,Y) that helps explain why augmentation sometimes helps despite symmetry breaking (task-irrelevant canonicalization) and sometimes hurts (task-relevant canonicalization, e.g. constructed QM7b dipole experiment, ModelNet40), producing a coherent, actionable practical flowchart (Figure 6).

Strong reproducibility effort: detailed appendices with architecture/training details, p-value computation via permutation tests, comparison to MMD with multiple kernels validating that the classifier-based metric agrees with alternative distance measures, and a public codebase.

Interesting follow-up investigations (local QM9/ModelNet40 neighborhoods, interpretability of the learned classifier's decision boundary via Mollweide projections, selective augmentation proof-of-concept) that add depth and open promising directions.
weaknesses: The task-dependent detection metric dclass(c(x), f(x)) is shown in the appendix to be quite sensitive to the choice of canonicalization network and classifier architecture (Table 6/7), undermining confidence in this variant; the paper pivots to the direct-prediction metric t(pX,Y) partly for this reason, but the latter's dependence on the quality/naturalness of the chosen canonicalization function c(·) is still a source of potential bias not fully resolved.

The theoretical results are derived in a fairly stylized linear/ridge-regression setting with a specific 'minimal model' covariance structure (coupling modes with equal strength superpositions); while illuminating, the link between this idealized theory and the complex real datasets studied empirically is largely qualitative/suggestive rather than rigorously connected (e.g., no direct estimation of correlation strength or γc for QM9/ModelNet40 to confirm the theory's regime applies).

Some central explanatory claims (e.g., that local equivariance/motif symmetry explains why augmentation helps on QM9 despite global canonicalization) are explicitly acknowledged as hypotheses needing further validation, and the paper relies on indirect evidence (lower local m(pX)) rather than a controlled causal test.

The core classifier-based metric, while interpretable, is fundamentally a lower bound/approximation to a true distributional distance, and its numeric value is entangled with the capacity/generalization behavior of the chosen classifier family (acknowledged in Appendix B), which could limit precise comparability of m(pX) values across datasets of very different modality (point clouds vs. text vs. images).

The regression benchmarks intentionally use non-state-of-the-art architectures (older Graphormer, smaller e3nn models) to isolate the augmentation effect; while justified, this limits the direct practical takeaway for state-of-the-art model design and leaves open whether findings hold for stronger models.

strengths: Introduces a simple, interpretable, model-agnostic diagnostic (m(pX)) based on a two-sample classifier test to quantify distributional symmetry breaking, sidestepping the kernel-selection issues of prior non-parametric tests (Chiu & Bloem-Reddy).

Provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of invariant ridge regression under non-invariant covariance, in both under- and over-parameterized regimes, using deterministic equivalents/random matrix theory, showing precisely when data augmentation and test-time symmetrization help or hurt even for truly invariant ground-truth functions.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation across many benchmark domains (QM9, QM7b, ModelNet40, MNIST, rMD17, OC20, and an LLM materials dataset), consistently uncovering surprisingly high degrees of symmetry bias.

Uncovers a genuinely interesting and non-obvious empirical pattern: despite high symmetry bias in nearly all datasets, augmentation/equivariance helps in molecular property prediction (QM9/QM7b) but hurts in ModelNet40/MNIST, motivating further mechanistic investigation (task-dependent metric, locality analysis).

Proposes a complementary task-dependent metric t(pX,Y) and a locality analysis (local QM9/ModelNet40) that together provide a coherent, actionable explanation (and practical flowchart) for when equivariant methods are likely to help or hurt.

Very thorough supplementary material: ablations over architecture/hyperparameters showing robustness of the task-independent metric, p-value/MMD comparisons validating the classifier-based metric against alternative distances, and interpretability analysis of the trained classifier (Mollweide visualizations, instability analysis).

Formal proof (Section A.1) that gradient descent on equivariant networks under invariant loss is agnostic to per-datapoint orientation, providing clean theoretical motivation for why equivariant methods discard orientation information.
weaknesses: The task-dependent metric t(pX,Y) is comparatively ad hoc, depends on an arbitrary choice of canonicalization network c(·), and the appendix ablations (Table 6/7) show non-trivial sensitivity to network architecture, which somewhat undercuts its reliability as a diagnostic.

The connection between the ridge-regression theory (Section 4) and the deep-learning experiments (Section 5) is more qualitative/motivational than quantitatively predictive; the theory does not directly explain the specific QM9-vs-ModelNet40 discrepancy that is the empirical centerpiece of the paper.

Some central empirical puzzles (why equivariance still helps on already highly-canonicalized QM9) remain only partially explained via the locality hypothesis, which itself relies on a somewhat heuristic measure (predicting g from gx) and is left as future work.

The paper is very dense, combining two metrics, multiple theoretical regimes, and many datasets; the core narrative could be more tightly focused, and some results (e.g., selective augmentation in D.2.4) are only preliminary proofs of concept.

Baseline equivariant/non-equivariant architectures used for the regression tasks are not state-of-the-art (explicitly acknowledged by the authors), limiting the strength of practical conclusions about equivariant method performance.

The classifier-based metric's theoretical interpretation (Section B) relies on generic learning-theoretic bounds that are not particularly tight or specific to this setting, leaving the precise meaning of m(pX) somewhat informal for infinite groups.
